analysis.one_liner: Creates a federal HOME Corporation to invest billions in building and preserving affordable housing for low-income families.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan housing bill with 41 Senate cosponsors was referred to the Finance Committee, never acted on, and never received a vote before Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would set a national goal that every American family can afford decent housing, then back it with money and machinery. It creates a new federal HOME Corporation authorized to spend about $3 billion in fiscal 1990 and $3.1 billion in 1991, routed through states and cities to build, rehabilitate, and preserve housing for low-income families, with strict income targeting. It also expands rental assistance and public housing, funds homeless and supportive housing, extends rural housing programs, helps first-time buyers tap retirement savings for a down payment, and makes the low-income housing tax credit permanent. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Very low- and low-income renters, homeless people, elderly and disabled people needing supportive housing, public housing residents, rural households, and first-time homebuyers. Nonprofit community housing organizations get a guaranteed 10 percent set-aside of funds, and states and cities get new flexible investment money with a permanent housing trust fund they can reuse.

how_it_helps.text: Authorizes $3 billion for fiscal 1990 and $3.129 billion for 1991 through a new Government National HOME Corporation to invest in expanding the affordable housing supply.

Requires that at least 40 percent of investment funds go to housing occupied by very low-income families and at least 80 percent to low-income families, with rents capped at fair market levels and long-term affordability commitments.
Expands section 8 low-income rental assistance and authorizes new public housing development and replacement housing.
Authorizes McKinney Act grants to states and localities for emergency shelter, transitional housing, and permanent housing for homeless people.
Lets first-time homebuyers use IRA and 401(k) funds for a down payment and raises FHA loan ceilings to match regional median home prices.
Makes the low-income housing tax credit ceiling permanent and extends mortgage revenue bond authority through 1992.
Sets aside at least 10 percent of each jurisdiction's funds for housing built or owned by nonprofit community organizations.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, who fund the roughly $6.1 billion in two-year authorizations plus increased rental assistance and public housing budget authority. Participating states and cities must also contribute matching funds worth at least 25 percent of what they draw, though poorer jurisdictions can have that reduced during their first three years.

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes $3 billion in fiscal 1990 and $3.129 billion in 1991, plus increased budget authority for section 8 rental assistance and public housing, a substantial federal commitment at a time of budget pressure.

Each participating jurisdiction must contribute matching funds of at least 25 percent of the federal funds it draws, a real cost for state and local budgets, though the requirement can be reduced by up to 75 percent in a jurisdiction's first year.

The HOME Corporation may guarantee pools of affordable housing mortgages with the full faith and credit of the United States pledged to those guarantees, creating an open-ended federal liability if the mortgages default.
Allowing IRA and 401(k) withdrawals for down payments puts retirement savings at risk and could add demand that bids up home prices, partly undercutting the affordability goal.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are broad and well-targeted: funds are locked to very low- and low-income households, rents are capped, and affordability must be preserved for the life of the housing. The main costs are the federal price tag and the match on local governments, plus real if unquantified risk from full-faith-and-credit mortgage guarantees and from letting retirement accounts be tapped for home purchases. On balance it is a substantial, deliberately structured effort to expand affordable housing, and its design addresses many of the usual complaints about housing aid leaking to higher-income households.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in March 1989, sent to the Senate Finance Committee, and sat there until the Congress ended in January 1991, never reaching a vote or even a committee vote.

narrative.text: Senator Alan Cranston introduced the National Affordable Housing Act on March 15, 1989, with 28 original cosponsors including both Democrats and Republicans.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the day it was introduced.
The committee took no further action; no markup, committee vote, or floor vote is recorded for the rest of the 101st Congress.
The bill gathered 41 cosponsors, 31 of 55 Senate Democrats and 10 of 45 Senate Republicans, but never received a vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 1991.
A successor housing bill drawing on the same ideas passed later in the 101st Congress, creating the HOME program that still exists today.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: With this bill dead in committee, no new federal affordable housing investment program was created on these terms; lenders, developers, and local governments did not receive the new funding stream, and low-income renters and homeless people did not get the expanded assistance this bill promised. Most of its ideas resurfaced in a successor housing bill that did become law later in the same Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one; the bill died unused

for.name: Sen. Alan Cranston
for.role: U.S. Senator from California and bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 28 original cosponsors across both parties.

for.name: 10 of 45 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Sen. Alfonse D'Amato of New York.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Lloyd Bentsen
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day it was introduced and never reported it out; no committee action of any kind appears in the record for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was bipartisan, 31 of 55 Democrats and 10 of 45 Republicans, but the bill never reached a vote, so there is no roll call to show how the parties would have split.

industries.note: The bill reserves at least 10 percent of every jurisdiction's funds for housing developed, sponsored, or owned by nonprofit community organizations, making them a permanent channel for federal affordable housing money.

Expanded FHA insurance, extended mortgage revenue bonds, federal guarantees of affordable housing mortgage pools, and new construction and rehabilitation investment would all increase lending and building volume.

industries.industry: State and local housing finance agencies
industries.note: The bill guarantees obligations issued by state and local housing finance agencies backed by affordable housing mortgages and funds capacity-building for state and local agencies.

The bill directs jurisdictions to maximize private-sector participation in financing and developing affordable housing, creating subsidized business for developers, though income targeting and rent caps limit what they can charge.
